# Content pack: Why small teams ship faster

## Tweet thread
1. Small teams ship faster. Not because they work harder — because of structure. Here's the breakdown (1/5)
2. 3 people share 3 communication pairs. 10 people share 45. Most of a larger team's extra energy goes into staying aligned, not into the work itself. (2/5)
3. Small teams can't afford process theatre. When 4 people can see the whole system, coordination happens in the code and in a 2-minute hallway conversation — not in a status doc nobody reads. (3/5)
4. The reason people miss: small teams make smaller decisions. Try something Tuesday, abandon it Thursday. Speed is a consequence of cheap reversal, not of typing quickly. (4/5)

## LinkedIn post
Small teams ship faster — and it has almost nothing to do with effort.

Three people share three communication pairs. Ten people share 45. That's not a small efficiency gap; it's a structural tax. Most of the extra energy in a larger team disappears into staying aligned, not into the work itself.

The second reason is the absence of theatre. A small team can't afford a weekly status meeting whose only output is a document nobody reads, or a design review built to distribute blame. When four people can see the whole system, coordination happens in the code and in a two-minute hallway conversation. Process gets layered on when trust or context runs out.

But the reason people often miss is this: small teams make smaller decisions. A large team has to plan far ahead, because reversing course means re-aligning everyone. A small team can try something on Tuesday and abandon it on Thursday. Speed there is a consequence of cheap reversal — not of typing quickly.

None of this means small is always right. Some problems genuinely need more hands, and a team of four can't staff an on-call rotation without burning out.

The practical question, then, isn't "how do we grow?" It's "what's the smallest team that can own this end to end?"

## Newsletter
## Why small teams ship faster

Most of the answer isn't effort. It's structure.

Communication paths scale exponentially: three people share three pairs, ten people share 45. Most of a larger team's extra energy goes into staying aligned, not into the work.

Small teams also can't afford process theatre. When four people can see the whole system, coordination happens in the code — not in a weekly status meeting whose only output is a document nobody reads.

The third reason is the one people miss: small teams make smaller decisions. They can try something on Tuesday and abandon it on Thursday, so they take more shots and learn faster.

**Takeaway:** the question isn't "how do we grow?" — it's "what's the smallest team that can own this end to end?"
